# A Quantum Leap? ## Summary First Quantum's proposed acquisition of Inmet Mining was first announced in November 2012 – a transaction valued at ~C$5Bn in equal split of cash and equity. This acquisition would more than double First Quantum's copper reserves and boost its copper production to become the sixth largest copper mine producer by 2017 overtaking Rio Tinto. Through Cobre Panama in Latin America and Inmet's other operating assets in Europe, First Quantum will be further diversified away from the central Copperbelt in Africa. First Quantum consolidated operating cash flow pre-tax will grow from ~US$2Bn to ~US$3Bn by 2018, and better position the company to competitively pursue further organic growth and M&A and rank itself as one of the key copper mine producers against the diversified majors of this world. Metals Cost Service Insight ## Introduction On 28th November 2012, First Quantum Minerals made an offer to acquire Inmet Mining for C$70 per Inmet share, consisting of 50% cash and 50% First Quantum shares and valuing the company at just under C$5Bn. Inmet's board promptly rejected the proposal stating it was "highly conditional". First Quantum has since amended its offer to C$72 per Inmet share. First Quantum has completed several other M&A over the past few years including the Kevitsa copper-nickel project in Sweden, the Ravensthorpe nickel project in Australia, the Sentinel copper and Enterprise nickel projects in Zambia and the Haquira copper project in Peru. Inmet on the other hand has not recently participated in any major M&A transactions except for its acquisition of Cobre Panama in 2008 and the proposed merger with Lundin Mining in late 2010 which fell through. The company's efforts have been focused on the US$6.2Bn Cobre Panama project which is now fully permitted and financed. We have identified three key strategic elements behind this proposed acquisition: #### **Size Matters** First Quantum's acquisition of Inmet will more than double reserves, and boost its copper mine production above Rio Tinto's by 2017 to be the 6th largest copper mine producer in the world. Consolidated operating cash flow pre tax would rise from ~$2Bn to ~$3Bn by 2018. The chart below illustrates where First Quantum (FQM) would be in terms of mineral reserves, copper grade and annual production in 2018, including and excluding Inmet assets. #### **Committed to Copper** With Freeport McMoRan's recent proposal to diversify into oil, First Quantum would be the largest publicly-traded company with a primary focus on copper. BHP Billiton, Anglo American, Xstrata and Rio Tinto are strategically diversified into the bulk commodities (coal and iron ore) in addition to copper and other base metals. ### **Base Case & Probable Reserves****1** **(Bubble Size = equity copper mine production in 2018)** 1.

Until recently, First Quantum was focused in the central Copperbelt of Zambia and DRC. The company's exposure to the DRC was consistently regarded by the market as politically high-risk and in 2009 the government cancelled First Quantum's mining concessions for Frontier and Kolwezi Tailings. First Quantum's presence in Zambia will remain significant – the Sentinel copper deposit in Zambia, now a base case project in construction, is projected would more than triple the company's production to 760kt in 2018 from 260kt in 2012. ## Cobre Panama: A Closer Look First Quantum's proposed acquisition of Inmet Mining is undoubtedly all about the Cobre Panama project, which is one of the largest undeveloped copper reserves in the world (see chart below). Inmet's presence in Panama dates back to the 1990s (see Development History table below) and its current ownership is 80% with the balance held by Korea Panama Mining Corp (KPCM). Earlier in 2012 KGHM completed a similar transaction involving Quadra FNX and its 55%-owned Sierra Gorda project in Chile – an operating company with a large porphyry deposit. #### **It's Big** Along with Cerro Colorado (owned by the Government of Panama) and the Kerr Sulphur Mitchell (KSM) project in Canada, Cobre Panama is one of the few large projects which are not owned by a major producer (i.e. Codelco, Freeport, BHP, Anglo, Rio Tinto and the likes). The chart below shows for each project the range of break-even copper price at a 12% discount rate,

also known as the project incentive price (PIP). #### **It's Expensive** The estimated capex for this project was initially quoted as US$1Bn for a 120kt/d operation back in 1998; this figure was revised for the same scope to US$1.7Bn in 2006, US$3.5Bn in 2008 and then to US$6.2Bn in 2012. The project at the time of writing is fully financed with US$0.3Bn incurred, US$3.3Bn in cash, US$1.0Bn from precious metals stream, US$1.2Bn from JV partners KPMC and the balance of US$0.4Bn to be sourced from Inmet's operating cash flow. One advantage that First Quantum would bring to the table is its internal expertise in project development. The company's prior projects have consistently been developed at the lower end of the project capital intensity compared with other concurrent projects, and a downwards revised capex estimate from First Quantum is possible. However, Cobre Metals Cost Service Insight - January 2013 Page 3 of 6 Metals Cost Service Insight Panama is on a significantly larger scale than the company's past projects and with a proportionately large capital commitment. #### **It's in Panama** Another important note is with regard to managing social and political relationships in Panama. Inmet's presence in the country dates back to the 1990s under Minnova (later Metall and then Inmet) and it would be important for First Quantum to inherit the important local connections to ensure that project development progresses smoothly regardless of a change in ownership. Government approved the project ESIA in 2011 but we note that mining is a nascent sector for this country. Consequently its mining laws and environmental regulations are likely to evolve as the sector grows and matures. Panama's economy relies on international maritime trade through the Panama Canal, a 77km-long transport channel that connects the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans. Some have viewed this existing dependence on global trade as an affirmation that Panama will maintain good relationships with other foreign entities. However, it has consistently been of importance to countries to have a sense of national ownership over its natural resources and this remains a risk to operating in Panama. ### **Cobre Panama is one of the largest undeveloped copper reserves*** in the world** 18

_od Mackenzie_| Metals Cost Service Insight - January 2013 Page 4 of 6 Metals Cost Service Insight ## Grow or Perish That every living thing must grow or perish certainly applies to the mining industry. Consolidation has been a consistent theme in the copper mining industry; copper mine production has increased 175% over the past three decades, and over this period the top 15 companies have consistently accounted for ~65% of the global copper mine production. This is not surprising when one considers that porphyry deposits account for around ~60% of total copper mine production – these are large, low-grade ore bodies typically located at high altitudes in mountain ranges and depend on economies of scale to be profitable. Consequently porphyry deposits today have initial capex requirements in the order of billions of dollars, a sum that can be financed only by an established producer. Cobre Panama is but one example of such deposits. Consolidation through M&A is a quicker way to grow the production portfolio, and this is especially true today when even the established producers are struggling with environmental and social permits for greenfield and brownfield projects – examples include Xstrata's Frieda River and Tampakan, Anglo American's Quellaveco and Pebble, BHP / Rio Tinto JV Resolution Copper. Consequently, it is increasingly more attractive to buy an operating mine, or a project once it is permitted and ready for construction. Also, some brownfield expansion projects are becoming more expensive and comparable to greenfield projects, with examples to include BHP's Olympic Dam, BHP / Rio JV Escondida and Codelco's Chuquicamata UG and Andina. We believe M&A will continue for the copper producers, with recent examples including the proposed merger of Xstrata and Glencore, and Freeport McMoRan's diversification into oil. Our view is that First Quantum's proposed merger with Inmet will grow the company and place it in a better financial position to pursue further M&As, but at the same time potentially mak

e it too large an M&A target for the diversified majors. This is similar reasoning as to why we believe Freeport has not been a take-over target – that its copper exposure is too large to maintain the strategic diversification ratio with coal, iron ore and other base / precious metals for the likes of BHP Billiton and Anglo American. ### **Equity Mine Production in 2012** 1,800 90%

Metals Cost Service Insight - January 2013 Page 5 of 6 Metals Cost Service Insight ## Conclusion First Quantum's acquisition of Inmet would further diversify its geographic presence away from the central Copperbelt in Africa and accelerate its growth to become the sixth largest copper mine producer by 2017, overtaking Rio Tinto. It would be the largest publicly traded company with a primary focus on copper assuming Freeport McMoRan's proposed diversification into oil proceeds to completion. Cobre Panama would be First Quantum's first porphyry copper project in Latin America (assuming it proceeds before Haquira), an important milestone for the company to grow its size and global footprint. Consolidated operating cash flow pre tax would rise from ~US$2Bn in 2012 to ~US$3Bn by 2018. In an environment where projects are becoming increasingly expensive to develop, First Quantum would benefit from the increased operating cash flow to competitively pursue further organic growth and M&A and rank itself as one of the key copper mine producers against the diversified majors of this world. **Sophie H.
